br1-count-the-cost.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Podcast power or proof? Before you believe a business claim, sort it. A fact claim (a company did a thing on a date) is settled by a record, such as the company's own annual report. A frame claim (this is a war) is a lens, neither true nor false. A cause claim (this is why one won) can only be answered by the actors' own words and deeds at the time. Here is how the Word sets that order.
br1-count-the-cost.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Podcast power or proof? A podcast like Business Wars is a doorway, not the record. Sort each claim before you judge it. Fact claims go to the record, the way Netflix's own annual report settles when it was incorporated. Frame claims are lenses: ask what they show and what they hide. Cause claims wait on what the actors said and did at the time. Count the cost first (Luke 14:28), name the record, then decide. That is the diligent way, not the way of the simple who believe every word (Proverbs 14:15).

teen.open: How do you know if a podcast is telling you facts? Sort each claim first: is it a fact, a frame, or a cause?
teen.close: So a podcast is a door, not proof. Facts get checked against records, frames are just ways of looking, and causes need what people actually said and did.

senior.open: The title asks how to tell a podcast's persuasion from proof. Sort every claim as fact, frame, or cause before judging, and let the record settle the facts.
senior.close: So count before you conclude. A fact claim is settled by the company's own record, a frame is a lens to weigh, and a cause waits on the actors' own words and deeds. Name the record, then decide.

br2-go-to-the-filing.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How do you check a company's story against its official record? Go to what the company filed itself. A public company must write its own record: an annual report on Form 10-K every year, signed by its officers, and a current report on Form 8-K when something material happens. All of it is public, free, and dated. Here is how Netflix and Blockbuster told their own stories.
br2-go-to-the-filing.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How do you check a company's story against its official record? Find the filing. Netflix's 10-K states in its own words when it was incorporated and whom it competed with. Blockbuster's exhibit of September 23, 2010 named its going-concern risk and its chapter 11 cases, on the day. Blockbuster filed its own ending. Before you repeat what a story says a company did, find where the company said what it did, and you have done a king's work of searching out a matter (Proverbs 25:2).

teen.open: How do you check a company's story? Look up what the company filed about itself, because public companies must write their own record.
teen.close: So skip the retelling and find the filing. Blockbuster wrote its own ending in a 2010 report, and anyone can read it.

senior.open: The title asks how to test a company's story against the official record. The answer is the company's own required filings, the annual 10-K and the current 8-K, which are public and dated.
senior.close: So before repeating a story about a company, find where the company said it in its own filing. Blockbuster's own exhibit of September 2010 told its ending plainly, on the day.

You go and find the second witness: the other party's filing, the regulator's docket, the court's finding. Then you say only what the records establish together. The Boeing and Airbus disputes show how.
br3-two-or-three-witnesses.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Two sides, two accusations: how would you know who is telling the truth? You read both records. DS316 alone leaves you sure of Airbus's guilt; DS353 alone leaves you sure of Boeing's. Together they establish that both were formally accused, on named dates, over named measures, and that both went to a panel. They do not, on their own, settle who cheated. Each side seems just in its own cause until its neighbor searches it (Proverbs 18:17). Two witnesses, or it is not established.

teen.open: If two sides blame each other, how do you know who is right? You check both sides' records, not just one.
teen.close: So never repeat one side's story alone. Find the second witness, read both, and only say what both together show.

senior.open: The title asks how one can know the truth when two parties accuse each other. The rule of two or three witnesses answers it: corroborate before you repeat.
senior.close: So read both records before speaking. Each side alone seems just; together the Boeing and Airbus disputes establish the accusations and the panels, not a verdict on who cheated. Two witnesses, or it is not established.

br4-a-dramatization-is-not-a-record.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is that story staged or on the record? Ask one question: could a document carry this? A document, like Disney's 2009 release on buying Marvel, carries a date, a number, and a name, and stays where the company put it. A staged scene, however faithful, is appearance. The Word asks you to look well because the simple believe every word, while the prudent look well to their going (Proverbs 14:15).
br4-a-dramatization-is-not-a-record.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is that story staged or on the record? Ask whether a document could carry it. If a deposition, a letter, or a filing holds those words, find it and cite it. If only a script could carry them, enjoy the scene and never cite it. Yahweh's Word asks you to look well because a good scene becomes a repeated fact in a single hasty retelling (Proverbs 19:2), and righteous judgment looks past appearance (John 7:24). Thank the ones who built the doorway, then walk through it to the floor.

teen.close: So a dramatized scene is fun, but it is not proof. If a real document has it, cite that. If not, do not repeat it as fact.

br5-just-weights.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your scale honest? It is when you write your standard down before you weigh, read a rivalry by its conduct and its numbers rather than by which side you favor, and then say plainly what your findings do not settle. A court shows the method: the Microsoft case was weighed against a stated standard into 412 numbered findings. Here is how.
br5-just-weights.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your scale honest? The Microsoft court shows what an honest one looks like: a standard stated first, then 412 numbered findings of conduct and numbers, such as monopoly power and a market share above ninety percent for a decade. And it knows its limits: those findings do not judge whether the suit was wise, whether the remedies were right, or the company's whole life. Weigh the same way. State your standard, number what you find, say what you have not found, and your weight is just (Proverbs 11:1).

teen.open: How do you judge a business fight fairly? Set your standard first, then look at what they did and the numbers, not which side you like.
teen.close: So an honest scale means standard first, conduct and numbers next, and being clear about what you still do not know.

senior.open: The title asks whether your scale is honest when you weigh a business rivalry. It is honest when the standard is stated first and the weighing follows conduct and numbers, not loyalty.
senior.close: So weigh as the court did: state the standard, number the findings, and mark plainly what they do not settle. That is the just weight the LORD delights in.

br9-follow-the-oil.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How did one barrel reach every price? Oil sits under every industry. In 1973 the production cuts took a barrel from $2.90 to $11.65, and the inflation oil caused was, in the Federal Reserve's own words, largely beyond the control of monetary policy. It reshaped a nation that in 1977 got 70 percent of its petroleum imports from OPEC and became a net exporter in 2020. And Standard Oil came to control ninety percent of the business. Here is the record.
br9-follow-the-oil.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. One barrel, every price: the record shows how. The shock: two oil crises, the first quadrupling the price of crude and the second tripling it, drove an inflation the central bank said was largely beyond its control. The nation: transportation burns about two thirds of its petroleum, and the country went from leaning on OPEC to net exporter. The company: Standard Oil's 1899 combination, controlling ninety percent, was adjudged a restraint of trade. Store wisely, as Joseph did, and remember who gives the power to get wealth (Deuteronomy 8:18).

teen.open: How can one thing like oil change every price? Almost everything runs on it, so when oil jumps, prices jump everywhere.
teen.close: So oil shook the economy in the 1970s, changed how America gets its energy, and helped one company control ninety percent of the business. And Yahweh is the One who gives the power to get wealth.
